passage:
The client demo was ten minutes away when the test server crashed. Avni leaned over Dhruv's desk. "Did you push the new build? Should I tell them we'll be late?"
"Can you not stand over me right now?" Dhruv snapped, without looking up. "I'm handling it."
Heat rushed into Avni's face. She walked back to her desk with her hands shaking, drafting a cold reply in her head. Then she noticed Dhruv's knee bouncing and his fingers jabbing the keyboard. He'd been at his desk since seven. Scared, she thought, more than rude.
After the demo, which started fifteen minutes late, she found him in the pantry. "That was a rough morning. Can we work out how we update each other when things break?"
Dhruv rubbed his face. "I was panicking. Sorry I bit your head off."

qa.q: What crashed just before the client demo?
qa.a: The test server crashed.

qa.q: How did Avni feel right after Dhruv snapped at her?
qa.a: Avni felt attacked and angry; heat rushed into her face and her hands shook as she drafted a cold reply.

qa.q: Which choice helped Avni most, and why?
qa.a: Avni waited until after the demo to talk, so both were calmer and could plan how to update each other instead of trading sharp words.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Dhruv?
qa.a: Dhruv was under heavy pressure and panicking, at his desk since seven with a broken server, so his sharp words came from fear.

grounding: A coworker stung by a stressed teammate's sharp reply sees the fear behind it and chooses a calmer conversation later.

passage:
By nine on Saturday, the kitchen of the Bandra café was roaring. Anand reached past Parveen for the chutney tray, and she spun round. "Move! Do you want to burn us both?"
Anand stepped back as if slapped. For the rest of the shift he chopped in silence, rehearsing a resignation speech. In the auto home he replayed her voice again and again.
But he also remembered her hands shaking as she plated, and the owner hovering by the pass all evening because a food critic was rumoured to be in.
On Sunday morning, before service, he found Parveen with her chai. "Yesterday hurt," he said simply. "I think you were scared, not that you hate me. Can we agree to call out when we pass behind each other?"
Parveen let out a long breath. "You're right. I was terrified. Let's do that."

qa.q: What did Anand reach past Parveen for?
qa.a: Anand reached past Parveen for the chutney tray.

qa.q: What did Anand feel in the auto on the way home?
qa.a: Anand felt hurt and angry, replaying Parveen's voice and rehearsing a resignation speech.

qa.q: What made the Sunday conversation work?
qa.a: Anand waited until both were calm, named his hurt simply without blaming, and suggested a practical call-out.

qa.q: What was the Saturday rush like for Parveen?
qa.a: Parveen was terrified, with the owner hovering and a critic possibly in the room, so her sharp words came out of fear.

grounding: A coworker hurt by a stressed teammate's sharp words later recognises the fear behind them and has a calmer talk the next day.

passage:
Subject: About yesterday
Hi Shreya,
I've been thinking about the release meeting since yesterday. When I asked about the test results, you said, 'Just do your job and stop asking me things.' Honestly, it stung. I went back to my desk feeling like I'd done something stupid in front of everyone, and my first thought was to go to our manager. But then I remembered you'd been here past midnight three nights running, and that the client had moved the deadline again. I don't think that reply was really about me. I'd still like to talk it over, calmly, once the release is out. Maybe Friday over chai? I want us to work well together, and I'd rather understand what was going on than stay annoyed.
Darshan

qa.q: What did Shreya say when Darshan asked about the test results?
qa.a: 'Just do your job and stop asking me things.'

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the release meeting?
qa.a: Darshan felt stung and embarrassed, as if having done something stupid in front of everyone.

qa.q: What makes Darshan's email a wise next step?
qa.a: It is honest about the hurt, links the reply to the late nights and deadline pressure, and proposes a calm talk after the release rather than escalating straight away.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Shreya might feel embarrassed about snapping but relieved to be offered understanding and a calmer conversation.

grounding: Shows a coworker who feels attacked by a stressed teammate's sharp reply, then recognises it came from pressure rather than contempt and suggests a calmer talk later.

passage: You know me, yaar, I'm Gurleen, I don't cry at work. But on Tuesday I did, in the stairwell. We had the client presentation at four, and at three-thirty Karthik looked at my slides and said, loudly, 'Did you even check these numbers? Unbelievable.' The whole team heard. My face went red and I thought, fine, he thinks I'm useless. I wanted to never speak to him again. Then, sitting on those stairs, I remembered him telling me last week that this account was his first big chance and he was terrified of losing it. So on Wednesday I waited till lunch was over and said, 'Yesterday really stung. Can we talk about it?' He went pale and said, 'I was panicking. It wasn't about you. I'm sorry.' We fixed the numbers together after that.

qa.q: What time was the client presentation?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel after Karthik's comment in front of the team?
qa.a: Gurleen felt humiliated and hurt, sure Karthik thought Gurleen useless, and wanted never to speak to him again.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen wait until Wednesday to raise it?
qa.a: Waiting until the pressure had passed let both of them speak calmly instead of reacting in the heat of the deadline.

qa.q: How did Karthik seem to see his own comment afterwards?
qa.a: He seemed ashamed, going pale and explaining that he had been panicking, not judging Gurleen.

grounding: Shows a coworker hurt by a stressed colleague's sharp remark who realises it came from fear rather than contempt, making a calmer talk possible the next day.

passage:
Monday: Leela, three weeks into the finance team, asked Chandrika where the audit files were. Chandrika didn't look up. 'Not now! Can't you see I'm drowning?' Leela went back to her seat with burning cheeks and typed half a complaint to HR before deleting it.
Wednesday: Leela noticed Chandrika eating lunch at her desk with shaking hands, phone pressed to her ear, saying, 'Yes, sir. Yes, by Friday. I know what's at stake.' Leela's anger cooled into something closer to worry.
Friday: After the quarter-end files went in, Leela brought two coffees over. Chandrika rubbed her eyes. 'About Monday. I was scared of missing the deadline and I took it out on you. I'm sorry.' They agreed that next quarter, Chandrika would put a red sticky note on her monitor on bad days, and Leela would send questions by message instead.

qa.q: What did Chandrika say when Leela asked about the audit files?
qa.a: 'Not now! Can't you see I'm drowning?'

qa.q: What did Leela feel on Monday, and how did it change by Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt hurt and angry enough to start a complaint; by Wednesday her anger cooled into worry when she saw Chandrika's pressure.

qa.q: What arrangement did they make, and why is it useful?
qa.a: A red sticky note on bad days and questions by message, which lets Leela avoid being snapped at and Chandrika keep focus.

qa.q: How does Chandrika seem to see her Monday reply looking back?
qa.a: She sees it as fear about the deadline spilling out on Leela, and she feels sorry for it.

grounding: Shows a coworker who feels attacked by a stressed teammate's sharp reply, then recognises it came from fear rather than contempt, leading to a calmer later conversation.

passage: Jasleen, you're upset that Arjun bit your head off before the audit? Sit. Let old Dhruv tell you something from my first bank job, when I was twenty-five. The night before a big inspection, I asked my senior, Mrs Fernandes, a simple question about a file. She turned round and snapped, 'Can't you do anything on your own?' in front of everyone. I felt attacked. My face burned, and I wanted to snap back or quit. Instead I went for a walk round the block. Next morning, after the inspection, she came to my desk, grey with tiredness. 'I was frightened we'd fail. It wasn't about you.' We talked properly over tea, and we worked together for eleven years. So talk to Arjun after the audit, not today.

qa.q: What did Mrs Fernandes snap at young Dhruv?
qa.a: 'Can't you do anything on your own?'

qa.q: How did young Dhruv feel when Mrs Fernandes snapped?
qa.a: Dhruv felt attacked and humiliated, face burning, wanting to snap back or quit.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Dhruv's story?
qa.a: Walking it off instead of snapping back, then talking over tea after the inspection when Mrs Fernandes explained she had been frightened.

qa.q: How did Mrs Fernandes feel when she snapped?
qa.a: She was frightened they would fail the inspection; her sharp words came from fear, not contempt.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls feeling attacked by a stressed teammate's sharp reply and learning that fear lay behind it.
